docs.text: Introduction Networking (L9) Welcome to this module, intended to cover Networking at L9, 10 credit equivalent. I plan and orchestrate my modules with 10 weeks of content, weeks 2-11. I reserve week 1 for introductions and getting started. The syllabus includes the following main content in weeks 2-11. Physical Network design LAN Network design WAN Network design Zones and perimeters The assessment material is based around doing all this work as a case study. I reserve week 12/13 for clean up at the end...or run over time if we need it. This is intended as a foundation module and has minimal prerequisites. It is assumed you already have an undergraduate degree in computing or a similar discipline. The material is thus pitched at people who can self-learn. I intend to provide the student with a solid grounding in network infrastructure requirements and practices both from a theoretical perspective and as an applied discipline. I began working with TCP/IP and Ethernet in the 1980s (!) and have been writing course and training material since the late 1990s. This module was written in 2015 and is updated annually, the most recent syllabus update was in 2022. If you are doing this module remotely, you need a good modern computer, review my "Getting Started notes now to understand what you need. In these documents, there are key terms. These will be italicized . You may need to look up these terms to get a full understanding of them. Commands are generally shown in bold . Reference Material If you are new to networking, I recommend Computer Networks, 6th edition, Published by Pearson (July 14, 2021) although earlier versions of the book are cheaper and almost perfect for understanding the underlying principles. Copyright The content of these notes are (c) John ORaw 2026. I have tried to acknowledge and cite sources, if you think I have missed crediting someone else's work, please contact me by university e-mail and I will remedy. If you find errors in my notes or something has been superseded without me noticing, please let me know. The pace of technological development assures that my notes have a very short shelf life. They are intended to be a starting point for your studies, not the end point.

docs.text: Practical Exercises There are particular approaches that an experienced network engineer will take when they are doing configurations, for a medium or large customer. I have some goals when I do this kind of work: Be as efficient as possible When I make a mess of things, recover as quickly as possible Be as accurate as possible; there is no room for error. One of the ways I have achieved this, is to not write configurations at the command line. When I'm working, I'm going to open notepad++ and I'm going to write my configuration into the editor with a minimum of comments. When I think the configuration is correct, I'll paste it into the network appliance and test it. For example, a good configuration for a normal client's access port might be # Configure technical clients int gi0/1 description Clients switchport access vlan 5 switchport mode access negotiation auto spanning-tree portfast edge spanning-tree bpduguard enable To configure a range of ports, I can just change the first line to int range gi0/1-24 Note that the exact syntax might change from switch to switch. Why do this with Notepad++? If I reset the switch, I lose nothing. If I must configure twenty switches in a consistent manner, I paste 20 times! This is not automation , but it is the first real step in Infrastructure as Code for my network. My equipment configuration is now recoverable, if I forget to save before resetting, or if a device fails. I have records of what I have done and a good script might last a few years and be usable on multiple projects before it needs updating. I have all my build documentation for the client. I could keep going, but you get the idea. When you are doing my practical exercises, use this methodology. You will discover by the time you have to do the first big network assignment, that you have almost no work to do!

docs.text: Writing Style The coursework associated with this module is intended to be done as an industry case study. From the start we will look at typical industry documents and you will submit those as you go along, modeling what we might do on a real project. Even though this material is delivered at postgraduate level, we are not going to treat this writing as academic. Write it as if your lecturer were a projects manager and you are the engineering consultant. I provide some guidance here on some of the typical documents I would provide on a networking project. Please use these as a guide when you were trying to produce documentation for this module.

docs.text: About the author I have been writing course content since the last millenium (sad but true!). Changing platforms has been the bane of my life. Moving my documents to an open format and to a technology that I can sync and save seems to be a good idea. And using a static site generator leaves me independent of any changes that come along to services in the future. After two years of experimentation, this is a new dedicated teaching account as of mid-2025. Retirement is hopefully not too far away! I want the notes to be available to my students after I retire, this is one way to do so. Contact me via my University e-mail address or via my LinkedIn account.

docs.text: Week 2 Last week's content was all good background. After that, We need to work through some of the theory relating to physical networking. You need to cover this in detail, the fist assignments are based on this content. In my notes on Layered Models, I referred to this as Layer 1 . In practical work, you will finally start configuring network equipment. There is a particular approach you must take, see my notes on Writing Style. If you take this approach, LAN assignments will be easy. If not... Study I cover some of the basics of Wired Networking next, this is the main content we need for Layer 1. Practical Work On campus or for e-delivery classes, I demonstrate how to access GNS3. I will not further describe that process here. This week, I need you to get familiar with using the Command Line (CLI) on network devices. A managed network device is an appliance computer, with a CPU, DRAM, and a boot device (flash). You need to understand the device and boot process. . In a real network, we need a scalable way to allow management access to equipment. Do the exercises on Authentication, Authorization and Accounting AAA Later Study If you run short on time now...these are items you need to know, but you do not need for the assignments. We touch on Wireless Networking , but very lightly. To finish with wireless networking, I also explain the ISM bands .

docs.text: Week 3 Over the next few weeks, we will study the design of Local Area Networks (LANs). Historically, we had many possible protocols at Layer 2, modern LANs are almost entirely based on Ethernet. At Layer 3/4, we also had many possible solutions, which have rationalized down to TCP/IP. We will begin this week by diving into Ethernet. We will also do practical exercises to better understand how Ethernet works. Study Begin by reading my introduction to Ethernet . Unless you understand where it came from, the terminology and operation of modern Ethernet will never make sense. As the technology developed, we utilized four families of Ethernet devices . You need to understand what they were and their operation principles. One of the problems we may have on an Ethernet is a network loop. We need to understand how to implement loop avoidance . Practical Work This week, carry out these exercises. Its time to start building switched networks . You must know how to correctly configure loop avoidance .

docs.text: Week 4 This week, we will finish with Ethernet for now. So far, we have seen how to provide physical ports, where we need network switches, how many ports, what speed. This week, we are going to look at logical network design, breaking up a flat Ethernet into Virtual LANs (VLANS) based on requirements to access applications, at specific security levels. If I were building a network right now, I would also configure Network Access Control (NAC) into the design. Do a little background reading on the topic, I'm not going to cover it for now. Study First understand VLANs. There are certain services we need on every LAN, I will discuss these here. Practical Work This week, carry out these exercises. Go through my practical work on VLANs . I show some simple technques for link aggregation. In practice, almost every host server uses something similar for redundant connectivity in data centre environments. Finally, I demonstrate Network Discovery , essentail for build, setup and test. Later Study If you run short on time now...these are items you need to know, but you do not need for the assignments. During setup and fault-finding, it is really useful to know some techniques for network discovery . We will examine this here. In a data center, there are few use-cases for WiFi , but we will cover some of the basics here. We have some use-cases for link aggregation , we will look at the basics here.

docs.text: Week 5 This week, we're going to address layer 3 and routing. For the moment, I'm going to concentrate on IPv4 and you will find subnetting a challenge. This doesn't require mathematical skill, it is algorithmic and it requires practice and experience. Study First, I introduce layer 3 . The next topic is to understand subnetting with IPv4 . I will do a live tutorial on this. Practical Work This week, carry out these exercises. To keep with the core requirements of the module, we are going to play with an OS running in Docker and do some simple scripting on network hardware. I need you to know how to do simple routing on a LAN with L2/L3 switches. There is a variation on LAN design, on sites which have a perimeter router, we call this router-on-a-stick . Later Study If you run short on time now...these are items you need to know, but you do not need for the assignments. docs.text: Week 6 To understand TCP/IP fully we need to discuss Layer 4 and we will do so this week. Everyone's Internet connection uses tricks to get around the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses, this is the right place to consider one of the mitigations for this, NAT and PAT. I also want to introduce dynamic routing and a simple routing protocol RIP. This week's notes and exercises finish the first part of the course. You should know how to build a small LAN and understand some of the practices for doing so. Study Read through my notes on Layer 4 . Practice I want you to try getting external Internet connectivity in your GNS3 simulations. Beware, this is untested in Azure Cloud. Once a network has any level of complexity, we need to be able to deal with routes. And once we have Internet connectivity, we need to understand static routes. Run through my exercises on static routes .

docs.text: Week 7 In the next part of this course, we're going to look more heavily at routing. In particular, we need to understand dynamic routing as it would be performed on LANs at all scales. And for the first time we need to consider the topologies of larger networks with greater complexity. And finally the architecture of our largest network, the Internet. Study The simplest dynamic routing protocol we will consider is RIP . It has a limited number of use cases these days, but we will also examine where it is an appropriate protocol for us to use. In contrast, we will also learn about OSPF , a protocol we could use for very large enterprises and for enterprise data centres. Practice In our exercises this week, we will utilize with both RIP and OSPF . Please make sure you understand where it is appropriate to use each. The assignments in the second half of this module normally require a competence with OSPF.

docs.text: Week 8 The largest network that we use is the Internet. At time of writing, it remains wholly reliant on the border gateway protocol (BGPv4). This week we want to gain an understanding of how the Internet works. And in data centres once we get to cloud scale and the biggest vendors, a type of internal BGP (iBGP) is also used almost exclusively. This week’s notes and exercises finish the first part of the course, on routing. Study Firstly, go through the theory on BGP . You should be beginning to understand how the Internet works as you complete this. Practice I get you to do some simple exercises in BGP this week. Be aware, what I am covering is trivial. In the professional world, this is the domain of the large carrier and the most expert skills I know in networking.

docs.text: Week 9 At this stage, you understand the switching and routing practice necessary to build many types of modern network. In this next section of the course, we need to look at how to create zones in our network and why and how to set up perimeters. This section of the course will emphasis the theory and practice of network security. At the risk of being cynical, many of the components of conventional network security just don't work. More than anything else, we need smart people who deeply understands the technical nature of our infrastructure and its vulnerabilities. Expect the next block in this course to be controversial! Study Before anything else, let's briefly discuss the concept of vulnerability and why it emerged so significantly in our industry. These notes were written before the emergence of AI/ML tools c.2024. I can't go any further in discussing security without introducing cryptography . I stay away from treating it as a formal discipline here. I need you to come away with the concepts and the terminology. There is a language to security and risk analysis, we need to introduce that and get to the point of having shared terminology .

docs.text: Week 10 This week we're going to dive into the appliances that we used to implement zones and perimeters, firewalls. This is technology that is only useful as long as we understand its limitations. I will discuss some of the use cases, where we locate firewalls internally on enterprise networks, pervasively in zones networks, and at security perimeters. Security cannot be taught as a static topic. It has been important all through this module that you use my notes as a base on which to work, not as the limit of your knowledge. And once we get to security, that limitation will never be more relevant. Once you finish this work, you can attempt the penultimate assignment for this module. Study Go through my notes on firewalls and the many variations and applications this week. Practice In our practical work, I want you to go through using one brand of commercial firewall, those produced by Fortinet . We will also talk about inter-connectivity between networks using VPNs. As part of this work, I will get you to access the teaching data centre via VPN. I will also introduce the concept of SD-WAN. In the Azure Labs VM, I will demo creating and configuring a Fortigate in Week 10.
